title: He is playing on his tablet and his time is up!
tldr: An eight-year-old who reports every minor rule-break isn't trying to be annoying; they are trying to master fairness and earn your approval. When they run to you with small violations, teach them the difference between keeping someone safe and getting someone in trouble. Thank them only when safety is at risk, and encourage them to handle the small stuff themselves.
scene: Your nine-year-old runs into the kitchen pointing: "Leo is playing Roblox and his thirty minutes was over ten minutes ago!"
You notice they are watching the clock like a hawk, waiting for their sibling to slip up.
So you are stuck between enforcing the limit — which rewards the policing — or letting it slide and looking completely unfair.
whats_going_on: At eight to ten, kids are obsessed with logic, justice, and absolute fairness.
They often report small things to get adult praise for being the good one who follows the rules.
They struggle to distinguish between a situation that is actually dangerous and one that is just annoying.
skip_these: Investigating the crime and handing out punishments on the spot.
Snapping at them to mind their own business.
Ignoring it entirely, which makes them feel like house rules do not matter.
try_this: Ask the safety question: "Is anyone hurt, or is anyone about to be hurt?"
Hand the problem back to them: "That sounds like a small thing you two can handle. What can you say to him?"
Set the boundary: "I only need to hear about it if someone is in danger."

activity.name: The Trash vs. Fire Test
steps: Draw a trash can and a fire engine on a piece of paper.
Give them age-appropriate scenarios, like a sibling using the wrong cup versus a sibling climbing on the high roof.
Ask them: "Does this need a firefighter to rescue someone, or can we just sweep it into the trash?"
activity.why_it_works: It gives logical older kids a visual scale to decide if a problem actually requires adult intervention.

remember: They are not trying to be a pest. They are trying to understand justice.
full_read:
Around eight to ten years old, a child’s brain undergoes a massive shift. They suddenly care deeply about rules, contracts, and absolute fairness. To them, a rule is not a loose guideline; it is a law of the universe. When they see a sibling or classmate bend that law, it feels like a personal affront to the order of their world. So they run to you, expecting you to act as the supreme court.

The temptation is to either snap at them for being a tattle-tale or to immediately go police the other child. But both approaches backfire. If you rush to punish the rule-breaker, you reward the reporting, and you will soon find yourself arbitrating twenty tiny disputes a day. If you tell them to stop complaining, they feel dismissed and confused because they thought they were helping you maintain order.

Instead, we need to teach them the distinction between reporting for safety and reporting for control. An eight-year-old is highly logical and entirely capable of understanding this boundary. They can learn that "telling" is what we do to protect someone from getting physically or emotionally hurt, while "tattling" is what we do just to get someone in trouble or to make ourselves look superior.

When they come to you with a complaint, put the responsibility back on them with a calm, neutral question. Ask them directly if anyone is in danger of getting hurt. If the answer is no, explain that this is a small problem they are strong enough to handle on their own.

By doing this, you stop acting as the household referee. You are showing them that while you will always step in to keep things safe, you also trust their growing independence to handle the small, everyday friction of living with other people.
